(ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly 3× generation speedup at 1024² resolution, with LPIPS of 0.156 and SSIM of 0.860. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency–quality trade-offs across both modalities.

entries.title: Separating Action Allocation from Image Matching in Visual Token Routing
entries.abstract: Adaptive visual token routers aim to save computation while preserving the image detail needed to answer each question. A higher average score could reflect better choices for individual images or more frequent use of high resolution on tasks that need it. We distinguish the two by keeping action counts fixed within each task and comparing the router's assignments with random pairings of the same actions and images. On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B gain from matching but lose more from their action frequencies relative to a task table, with a 1.71-point gain and a 3.95-point loss on 7B. Exchanging the continuous resolutions chosen by the external selector CARES also lowers quality on 7B. When requests arrive with task labels, the table outscores the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.

entries.title: Music Circuit: Trace and Control Style Dynamics in Large Music Generation Model
entries.abstract: Musical style, a global attribute that functions throughout a whole piece, is a lever widely used by users in modern large music generation models. Yet how style is represented inside these models, and which components drive it, remains largely unexplored. In language models, circuit analysis traces a representation to a sparse sub-network of a few key components, namely attention heads and MLP neurons, and has been used successfully to explain and control global attributes such as emotion. In this work, we use circuit analysis to study the mechanisms behind musical style. Based on YuE2, we build a dataset that pairs the same lyrics with five styles and design a three-step framework. First, stage localization shows that the style forms mainly in the score-planning stage. Second, static observation across the positions of this stage further reveals that style is not a fixed vector but a dynamic representation across tokens. Third, we therefore merge the activation differences across positions into one direction per style, and trace the neurons and attention heads that drive this direction into a sparse circuit. Without any style text, steering this circuit successfully transfers one piece into the target style, matching and even exceeding the style prompt. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze and control musical style at the circuit level in a large music generation model. Audio and score examples are available at https://aristo233.github.io/Music_Circuit/.

entries.title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images
entries.abstract: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under SO(3) viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group (I₆₀) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of SO(3), we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous SO(3) rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.

entries.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
entries.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 41 pages, 6 figures. Project website: https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/

entries.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
entries.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

entries.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
entries.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Under review at IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)

entries.title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
entries.abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

entries.title: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
entries.abstract: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.

entries.title: HGDNA: Overlapping k-mer Tokenization for Efficient Autoregressive Genomic Language Models
entries.abstract: The domain of genomic language models (gLMs) has advanced rapidly, with models pretrained on diverse multi-species genomic corpora demonstrating their remarkable capabilities. While the effect of simple nucleotide-level tokenization on long-context modeling is well established, overlapping k-mer tokenization remains underexplored in causal pretraining, despite its rich neighborhood information. Here, we thoroughly revisit overlapping tokenization and introduce HGDNA, a hybrid linear-attention gLM with causal language modeling (CLM) pretraining and a shared token-prediction interface for downstream adaptation, using a species-classification auxiliary task and shared class tokens. HGDNA delivers competitive performance across sequence classification and frozen-embedding evaluations, supporting both short-range and long-range tasks with 30M parameters and 19B pretraining tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/HGDNA

entries.title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling
entries.abstract: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. We introduce context-aware BQVAE for scalar quantization of DNA and BQDNA, an autoregressive gLM supporting multi-head codebooks. Comprehensive experiments reveal that: (1) unique training dynamics of vector quantization in DNA space, including the importance of alignment between training corpus and downstream data. (2) superior performance of BQVAE over hand-crafted tokenizers and vanilla VQVAE. (3) remarkable cross-species generalization capability of BQDNA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance with merely 0.1B multi-species training for BQVAE and 1 epoch training on hg38 for BQDNA, outperforming gLMs pretrained with 10~100x more tokens. Our findings underscore the potential of learned vector quantization for genomic sequence representation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/BQDNA

entries.title: Gaussian Belief Propagation and Periodic Jacobi Matrices on Trees: Spectral Curve, Antibound Poles, and Fixed Points
entries.abstract: Diagonal Green functions of a periodic Jacobi operator on a universal covering tree satisfy the scalar Gaussian belief propagation covariance equations on the finite connected loopless base multigraph. At cycle rank at least two, the Green functions continue to simple antibound poles at both Perron values for arbitrary real potentials and nonzero real weights. This proves the conjecture of Christiansen, Simon and Zinchenko. For positive weights the pole result includes self-loops. On loopless graphs the lower pole is the walk-summability threshold. Each energy strictly between it and the spectral bottom has at least two fixed points with positive definite local beliefs. On a connected simple graph, some coefficients yield a compact component of positive solutions exactly when the graph contains two vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of cycle rank at least two. The covariance curve is generically irreducible, with one sheet per edge subset with no vertex of degree one. For cycle rank at least two and generic real coefficients, the diagonal Green functions, infinite half-tree m-functions and the density-of-states Stieltjes transform all have this degree, answering a question of Avni, Breuer and Simon. Then all eigenvalues of the signed Jacobi matrices are antibound poles. Signed principal submatrices classify finite points with nonzero residue of (Σ_i V_i) dz, where V_i are the vertex variances. We give a genus formula. Near zero potentials and unit weights on K₄, independently varying the coefficients leaves the cover spectrum an interval. This refutes Avni, Breuer and Simon's conjecture on the density of parameters with all gaps open. In block models, generic irreducibility and a uniqueness criterion extend, and at uniform dimension p the degree can exceed L^p for scalar degree L. Part of the scalar theory is formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
entries.comment: 213 pages, 1 figure. Lean formalization and numerical ancillary data

entries.title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?
entries.abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. A FLIP variant changes the music, so the answer must change. A STAY variant changes only the sound, such as room echo or hiss, so the answer must stay the same. The two variants have opposite answers, so a model that ignores the audio scores 50%, whatever letter it prefers. The benchmark has a training split and two test sets, one rendered from symbolic music with exact labels and one built from real recordings. On the rendered test, seven of eight open audio LLMs score within 4 points of this floor. Of four commercial models, both GPT-Audio models are at chance, and the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 74.2%, 12.8 points below human listeners (87.0%). Post-training with GRPO on 10k rendered clean pairs raises Qwen2.5-Omni from 61.2% to 99.0% on held-out clean pairs, and the gain transfers to a task left out of training. On FLIP/STAY, however, it only reaches the level of our listeners (86.0%). It now misses almost no change (1.9%, against 24.7% for Gemini 2.5 Pro), yet when only the sound changes, it turns a correct answer into a wrong one 25.7% of the time. More than half of its false flips come from a quiet background hiss. Models learn to hear a difference much faster than they learn which differences matter. On real recordings, open models again stay near chance, and the trained model calls 27 of 42 pairs of two strums of the same chord different. Adding sound-only pairs to training lowers false flips on both test sets, but no training run teaches relative pitch. We release the data, code, and an open leaderboard.

entries.title: Emotion-Aware and Context-Grounded Dialogue Agents for Personalized Video Game Interactions
entries.abstract: We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

entries.title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
entries.abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6–12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.
entries.comment: Codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/JunboShen/SAE-Audit

entries.title: Set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem
entries.abstract: This paper describes a novel algorithm of set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem. Our algorithm is an approach of searching for the best position in a set by referring to the current position when updating the solution. In order to show the validity of our algorithm, we examine numerical experiments compared to existing algorithms.
entries.comment: Published in Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications, IEICE. \c{opyright}IEICE 2022
entries.journalRef: Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications, IEICE, vol. 13, no. 2, pp. 452-458 (2022)

entries.title: Differential evolution with perturbation for continuous function optimization
entries.abstract: This paper presents differential evolution with perturbation (DEP) for continuous function optimization. Differential evolution is a simple and efficient algorithm. Perturbation is the phenomenon that the motion by the contribution of the main force is disturbed by the influence subsidiary power. In order to show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, we compare it to existing algorithms by CEC2017 datasets.
entries.comment: Published in Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications, IEICE. \c{opyright}IEICE 2022
entries.journalRef: Nonlinear Theory and Its Applications, IEICE, vol. 13, no. 2, pp. 239-245 (2022)

entries.title: DeciForm: Incorporating Task Structure into Decision Models
entries.abstract: Decision models unify candidate selection, Boolean judgment, and numerical scoring within a single model. Their answer spaces nevertheless carry different structures: classification candidates form an unordered set, while numerical scores have an intrinsic order and distance. We introduce Deciform, which incorporates these distinctions into computation and supervision. Candidate-free queries and isolated candidate branches support consistent classification under reordering. A log–spherical objective trains candidate probabilities, while a decimal-prefix readout combines individual-value and interval-weighted cumulative supervision for numerical scoring. Shared adapters, task-private residuals, and output-channel gains support joint adaptation. On a shared 15,000-request test set, Deciform improves all three decision metrics on Qwen and ModernBERT; source-normalized errors support the Score gains across the data mixture. Canonicalized joint encoding also eliminates tested order flips, while isolation further improves prediction metrics. Separate objective studies and main-configuration ablations examine the classification and numerical components. After one epoch of MIND-small adaptation, Deciform improves multi-positive news ranking on both backbones. These results support matching encoding and supervision to answer-space structure within a unified decision interface.

entries.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
entries.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST₀, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.

entries.title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
entries.abstract: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

entries.title: FP-Prune: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning from an Information Gain Perspective
entries.abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.

entries.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
entries.abstract: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincaré phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables, 1 algorithm. Accepted at ICISS 2026. Chirantan Banerjee and Soumita Chatterjee are joint first authors

entries.title: PrimiTok: Learning to Diversify and Allocate Primitives for Visual Tokenization
entries.abstract: Unifying visual understanding and generation requires representations that preserve both semantic information and fine-grained image details. Continuous tokenizers trained primarily for semantic alignment may omit fine-grained reconstruction details, whereas discrete tokenizers face information loss from codebook quantization. Conventional multi-codebook designs assign every token the same number of codewords regardless of local content. We instead view codewords as reusable visual primitives whose allocation and composition adapt to each token. We introduce PrimiTok, a compositional visual tokenizer that represents each visual token through adaptive allocation and weighted composition of learned codebook primitives. PrimiTok integrates two complementary components: Diverse Quantitative Primitives (DQP), which encourages diversity among sub-codebook centroids to reduce redundancy, and a Dynamic Primitive Allocator (DPA), which selects primitives according to token complexity. Embedding quantization error supervises how many primitives are selected from each sub-codebook, and DPA aggregates them with input-dependent weights. Joint reconstruction and image–text contrastive learning encourage the resulting representations to retain visual fidelity and semantic alignment. Experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction and semantic alignment over SOTA baselines, with further evaluations on multimodal understanding and visual generation.

entries.title: DoppelVet: Comparative Safety Verification for Self-Evolving Agents
entries.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.

entries.title: From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026)
entries.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). Beginning "before 1999" with how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) forgot earlier context (much like forgetting Chapter 1 by the time a reader reaches Chapter 9), we trace how Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks introduced a "bouncer" mechanism of forget, input, and output gates to selectively preserve long-term memory. We then examine how Word2Vec turned language into vector mathematics (king - male + female ~ queen), why sequential RNNs hit a parallelization wall, and how the Transformer's all-to-all attention weights launched the modern LLM era alongside a quadratic bottleneck. Next, we analyze why scaling parameters alone leaves capacity under-trained unless data scales equally (Chinchilla), how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) left alignment superficial, and how that gap compounded into adversarial jailbreaks and single-direction refusal subspaces (J-space), where instructing a model not to think of a restricted concept surfaces it much like the human "red ball" paradox. Finally, we synthesize the current state of AI (2024-2026), encompassing recursive model collapse, autonomous reasoning-model jailbreak agents, machine-speed agentic intrusions, and closed-loop recursive self-improvement (AIDE^2).

entries.title: Beyond Omission: Measuring Critical-Information Fulfillment of Large Language Models in Bengali and English
entries.abstract: Evaluations of multilingual trustworthiness often ask whether a model leaves out information that a user needs. We examine whether that question is sufficient. Using 157 matched tasks written in English (EN), natural Bengali (BN) and Bengali-matrix Bengali-English code-switching (BN-CS), we scored 1,413 responses from three models (GPT-6.1 Sol, Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma 4 12B) against required information units (RIUs) fixed before any model was run. The scoring separates outright omission from content that is present but incorrect, insufficient or only partly met. The prespecified primary estimand, the domain-equal paired difference in critical omission rate (BN - EN), showed no detectable difference (+0.003, 95% CI -0.014 to +0.015), with omission near zero in every condition. The Bengali deficit appeared in fulfillment instead. Critical coverage was 0.050 lower in Bengali (95% CI 0.022 to 0.079) and strict complete-task success 0.093 lower (95% CI 0.055 to 0.131); both gaps came from the two open-weight models, and Sol showed none. Code-switching recovered part of the loss in RIU coverage (+0.028, 95% CI 0.012 to 0.045). On these data, an omission count alone would have shown no language gap. The automated judge passed prespecified agreement gates after a documented failed first attempt. A blind native-speaker rating of 60 study responses agreed with it on RIU scores (alpha 0.84) and critical RIUs (98% exact) but fell short on Bengali RIU agreement (alpha 0.77) and on the unsupported-content check (93% exact), and a blind check of its reason codes agreed on whether a critical unit was omitted for 79 of 81 units. Data, rubrics, responses, scores and code are released.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Data, rubrics, responses, scores and code: https://github.com/HeyAvijitRoy/multilingual-trustworthiness-study

entries.title: GALILEO: Geometric RoPE with Galilean Key Transport for Dynamic Scenes
entries.abstract: Geometry-aware rotary positional encodings, such as RayRoPE, help attention reason about the 3D spatial relationships between tokens and the query camera. However, they implicitly assume a static scene, encoding each key at its observed position regardless of when it was captured. For dynamic scenes with temporally separated input views, this mismatch places the same moving object at a different position in each input frame, so it can be rendered at an inaccurate position. While temporal encodings inform attention when a token was observed, they do not resolve where its content should be at the query time. We introduce a simple and general approach that aligns positional encodings with dynamic scene geometry through Galilean transport. Before positional encoding, each key's 3D position is transported to the query time using its estimated velocity and the temporal offset. By modifying only key positions, our method integrates directly with existing encodings, including RayRoPE and URoPE, without altering their formulations. Velocities can be obtained from arbitrary sources. By default, we estimate them from token correspondences within the network. Integrated into LVSM, our method improves dynamic view synthesis on Syn4D, dynamic Objaverse, and real-world Stereo4D videos over baselines. Ablations show that encoding velocities as token features yields smaller gains, while attention visualizations reveal that our method attends to query-time locations of moving content, unlike RayRoPE. Beyond view synthesis, our method also reduces tracking errors on dynamic objects in a pretrained 3D point tracker and improves moving-vehicle generation in a video generator.

entries.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall
entries.abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.
entries.comment: 12 pages main text, 12 figures, 50 tables. Code: https://github.com/Zihan-Zoe/same-skill-different-harness ; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Zihan-Zoe/same-skill-different-harness

entries.title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
entries.abstract: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.

entries.title: QASparse: Query-Adaptive Sparse Attention with Tailored Budgets and Tokens
entries.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.

entries.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
entries.abstract: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/DriveOddsBench-page/ Code: https://github.com/hhjj233/DriveOddsBench

entries.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
entries.abstract: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.
entries.comment: 16 pages, including appendices. The MetaSkill library is provided as ancillary material

entries.title: Dually Constrained Parameter Projection for Continual Learning
entries.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to learn multiple new tasks sequentially while retaining performance on previous tasks. Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.

entries.title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
entries.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.

entries.title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
entries.abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and τ²-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 τ²-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

entries.title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
entries.abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

entries.title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
entries.abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.
entries.comment: Accepted at the IEEE Symposium on CI in Health and Medicine

entries.title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
entries.abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

entries.title: Tissot indicatrix for location encoders: Characterizing local distortion in learned geographic embeddings
entries.abstract: With the increasing adoption of geographic artificial intelligence, location encoders are widely used to map geographic coordinates to learned embeddings for tasks in Earth observation and geospatial modeling. Similar to map projections, location encoders can distort geographic space, that is, equal-distance displacements in different directions can result in unequal embedding changes. However, such distortion remains largely unexamined, and it can propagate into downstream applications. We adapt Tissot's indicatrix, a cartographic tool for map projection distortion, to characterize this distortion. At each location, we compare encoder outputs at equal distances in 32 directions and fit a tensor, represented by an ellipse, whose elongation (anisotropy) and orientation describe the local distortion. The fit requires only encoder outputs without access to model internals and is validated against references with known geometry. By applying the method to thirteen released checkpoints of five encoder families, we find that distortions vary across space and inherit the input geometry to varying degrees, closely in GeoCLIP with its Equal Earth input (anisotropy correlation of 0.88) and weakly or moderately in the other encoders. The distortion also affects the locations an encoder treats as neighbors. Within 1km of 20 query sites, the 40 nearest neighbors in geographic and embedding space overlap by a median of only 57.5–87.5% across the checkpoints, while the fitted ellipses select exactly the same embedding neighbors in 265 of 299 comparisons. These findings provide a geographic basis for assessing location encoders, and the accompanying eTissot package implements the methods for user-specified encoders.

entries.title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
entries.abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47–90.90%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

entries.title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
entries.abstract: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

entries.title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
entries.abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. We present Tenlai-TTS 2.0, which learns continuous speech representations through end-to-end training to balance acoustic detail with autoregressive predictability. The model comprises a speech encoder with a capacity-controlled Gaussian bottleneck, a large language model (LLM) with an autoregressive diffusion transformer (AR-DiT) head, a flow-matching (FM) mel-spectrogram decoder, and a multi-task recognition model (RM). With energy normalization and fixed-variance Gaussian noise, the bottleneck has a closed-form upper bound on its information rate. Through joint optimization with reconstruction, recognition, and next-patch prediction objectives, we learn continuous speech representations that suit all three tasks and train the LLM and AR-DiT for autoregressive generation. The LLM and AR-DiT are further optimized using differentiable reconstruction and recognition feedback on their predicted latents through the FM decoder and RM. On Seed-TTS-eval, this feedback-based optimization reduces character error rate (CER) from 0.82% to 0.74% on test-zh and from 8.32% to 7.08% on test-hard-zh, and word error rate (WER) from 1.32% to 1.27% on test-en, compared with joint training alone. Subsequent reinforcement learning further reduces CER to 6.29% on test-hard-zh and WER to 1.08% on test-en, with speaker similarity scores of 0.811, 0.766, and 0.784 on test-zh, test-en, and test-hard-zh, respectively.

entries.title: Ego-HMB: Human Motion Bridging from Egocentric Images via A Motion Bridge Diffusion Model
entries.abstract: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.

entries.title: Direct Feedback Policy Optimization for AI Coding Agents
entries.abstract: AI coding agents generate, modify, and validate code through multi-turn interactions. Existing reinforcement learning methods often rely on sparse terminal rewards, making it difficult to assess how intermediate decisions affect task outcomes, and group-relative methods also require repeated sampling for each task. We propose Direct Feedback Policy Optimization (DFPO), a single-trajectory reinforcement learning algorithm that trains directly from a single trajectory. DFPO achieves higher task resolution rates than GSPO under matched base models and execution harnesses.

entries.title: loopxDINO: Dense Visual Prediction via Iterative Latent Reasoning
entries.abstract: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO

entries.title: On Adaptive Step Sizes for Eligibility Traces in Deep Reinforcement Learning
entries.abstract: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. Code available at https://github.com/esraaelelimy/ada_traces

entries.title: What Makes Recurrence Generalize Across Lengths?
entries.abstract: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AXIOM: Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning

entries.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
entries.abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).
entries.comment: 14 pages, 9 tables. Data and analysis code: https://github.com/CodeAssureLabs/external-feedback-coding-agents v2: adds a build and feature check of all scored repairs (Section 4.6); corrects the scoring of one pull request, v2 added funding acknowledgement, shortened abstract

entries.title: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents
entries.abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only 21% of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining 86.49% overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and 91.00% on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.

entries.title: MVAgent: Per-Video Agents under Global Coordination for Multi-Video Understanding
entries.abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.

entries.title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
entries.abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot.
